nodes.title: Statements and implication
nodes.summary: A statement has a truth value. An implication says that whenever P holds, Q holds.
nodes.detail: To prove P implies Q, assume P and justify Q. The reverse implication requires its own argument.
nodes.proof: If n is divisible by 4, then n is even: n=4k=2(2k).
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Sets and membership
nodes.summary: A set collects objects; membership says an object belongs to that collection.
nodes.detail: Two sets are equal when they have exactly the same members. Prove both inclusions.
nodes.proof: A ∩ B = B ∩ A. An object belongs to either side exactly when it belongs to both A and B.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Functions
nodes.summary: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain.
nodes.detail: Injective means distinct inputs have distinct outputs. Surjective means every target is reached.
nodes.proof: The function f(x)=2x on the real numbers is injective: 2a=2b implies a=b.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Proof by contradiction
nodes.summary: Assume the negation of your claim and derive something impossible.
nodes.detail: State the negation precisely, then identify the incompatible conclusions.
nodes.proof: There is no largest integer. If N were largest, the integer N+1 would be larger.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Mathematical induction
nodes.summary: Prove a starting case and a rule that advances one case to the next.
nodes.detail: Induction on positive integers needs both the base case and the implication from n to n+1.
nodes.proof: 1+…+n=n(n+1)/2. Base n=1 holds. Adding n+1 to the formula gives (n+1)(n+2)/2, the next case.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Integers and divisibility
nodes.summary: Integers are whole numbers; a divides b when b is an integer multiple of a.
nodes.detail: Divisibility replaces numerical size with multiplicative structure.
nodes.proof: If a divides b and b divides c, write b=ak and c=bℓ. Then c=a(kℓ), so a divides c.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Rational numbers
nodes.summary: A rational number is a ratio of two integers with nonzero denominator.
nodes.detail: Different fractions can represent the same number. Arithmetic must preserve nonzero denominators.
nodes.proof: The sum of a/b and c/d is (ad+bc)/(bd). The numerator is an integer and bd is nonzero, so the sum is rational.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Prime numbers
nodes.summary: A prime is an integer greater than one whose only positive divisors are one and itself.
nodes.detail: Prime factorization turns multiplication into information about prime factors.
nodes.proof: There are infinitely many primes. If p₁,…,pₖ were all primes, N=p₁…pₖ+1 has a prime divisor. None of the listed primes divides N, a contradiction. Here we use that every integer greater than one has a prime divisor.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Modular arithmetic
nodes.summary: Two integers are congruent modulo m when their difference is divisible by m.
nodes.detail: Fix a positive modulus m. Congruence records remainders rather than full integers.
nodes.proof: If a≡b and c≡d mod m, then a+c≡b+d: (a+c)−(b+d)=(a−b)+(c−d), a sum of multiples of m.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Counting and bijections
nodes.summary: Count a collection by matching it with another collection of known size.
nodes.detail: A bijection is an invertible function and preserves the size of finite sets.
nodes.proof: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets: each element has two independent choices, included or excluded.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Graphs and paths
nodes.summary: A graph consists of vertices and edges; a path follows edges between vertices.
nodes.detail: Graph properties describe connections independently of how a picture is drawn.
nodes.proof: In a finite undirected graph without loops, the sum of degrees equals twice the edge count: each edge contributes once at each endpoint.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Inequalities and bounds
nodes.summary: Bounds tell us how large or small a quantity can be without finding it exactly.
nodes.detail: State the domain and sign conditions before multiplying or dividing inequalities.
nodes.proof: For real a,b, (a−b)²≥0 gives a²+b²≥2ab. Equality holds exactly when a=b.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Sequences
nodes.summary: A sequence is a function whose inputs are positive integers.
nodes.detail: Think of aₙ as the value at stage n. A pattern in the first few terms is not a proof about all terms.
nodes.proof: The sequence aₙ=1/n is decreasing because n+1>n>0 implies 1/(n+1)<1/n.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Limits and convergence
nodes.summary: A sequence converges when its terms eventually stay arbitrarily close to a fixed value.
nodes.detail: For every ε>0 there must be an N such that n≥N implies |aₙ−L|<ε.
nodes.proof: 1/n tends to zero: given ε>0 choose an integer N>1/ε. For n≥N, 0<1/n≤1/N<ε.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Continuity
nodes.summary: Small changes in input produce small changes in output, at the point under consideration.
nodes.detail: At a, for every ε>0 choose δ>0 so |x−a|<δ implies |f(x)−f(a)|<ε.
nodes.proof: f(x)=2x is continuous: choose δ=ε/2. Then |f(x)−f(a)|=2|x−a|<ε.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Derivatives
nodes.summary: A derivative measures the limiting rate of change at a point.
nodes.detail: The derivative is the limit of (f(x+h)−f(x))/h as nonzero h tends to zero, when it exists.
nodes.proof: For f(x)=x², the quotient is 2x+h. Its limit as h tends to zero is 2x.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Integrals
nodes.summary: Integration adds contributions over a region, often through limits of finite sums.
nodes.detail: For Riemann integration on an interval, refine partitions and compare upper and lower sums.
nodes.proof: For a constant c on [a,b], every Riemann sum is c times the sum of interval widths, hence c(b−a).
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Vectors and linear combinations
nodes.summary: Vectors can be added and scaled; linear combinations mix these operations.
nodes.detail: A vector space must obey the vector space axioms over a specified field.
nodes.proof: The span of u and v is closed under addition: (au+bv)+(cu+dv)=(a+c)u+(b+d)v.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Linear maps
nodes.summary: A linear map preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication.
nodes.detail: Matrices represent linear maps after bases are chosen.
nodes.proof: The kernel is closed under addition: if T(u)=T(v)=0, then T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)=0. It also contains zero and is closed under scaling, so it is a subspace.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Norms and distances
nodes.summary: A norm measures vector length; a metric measures distance between two points.
nodes.detail: A metric must be nonnegative, symmetric, zero only on equal points, and satisfy the triangle inequality.
nodes.proof: Given a norm, d(x,y)=‖x−y‖ satisfies the triangle inequality because x−z=(x−y)+(y−z). The other metric axioms follow from the norm axioms.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Groups and symmetry
nodes.summary: A group combines elements associatively, with an identity and an inverse for every element.
nodes.detail: Symmetries form groups under composition. Group operations need not commute.
nodes.proof: An identity is unique: if e and f are both identities, then ef=f because e is an identity, and ef=e because f is one. Thus e=f.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Rings and polynomials
nodes.summary: Rings support addition and multiplication; polynomials encode finite algebraic expressions.
nodes.detail: The exact ring axioms, including whether an identity is required, must be stated.
nodes.proof: In any ring, a·0=0: a·0=a(0+0)=a·0+a·0. Subtract a·0 in the additive group.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Open sets and topology
nodes.summary: Topology describes neighborhoods and continuity without requiring a numerical distance.
nodes.detail: A topology contains the empty and whole sets, is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections.
nodes.proof: An arbitrary union of open metric balls is open: each point belongs to one ball and has a sufficiently small ball around it contained in that ball. The triangle inequality justifies the containment.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Compactness
nodes.summary: Compactness means every open cover has a finite subcover.
nodes.detail: Compactness can turn local information into a finite global argument. It does not mean finite cardinality.
nodes.proof: Every finite set is compact: for each of its finitely many points choose one member of an open cover containing it. Those finitely many members cover the set.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Measure and probability
nodes.summary: A measure assigns sizes to sets, adding over disjoint countable unions.
nodes.detail: A probability measure has total mass one. Specify the measurable sets before assigning probabilities.
nodes.proof: P(Aᶜ)=1−P(A): A and its complement are disjoint and their union is the whole sample space, so additivity gives P(A)+P(Aᶜ)=1.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Expectation
nodes.summary: Expectation is the average of a random variable weighted by probabilities.
nodes.detail: For finite random variables, compute a sum of value times probability. Infinite cases need integrability conditions.
nodes.proof: For finite random variables, E[X+Y]=Σω(X(ω)+Y(ω))P(ω)=E[X]+E[Y] by distributing a finite sum. No independence is needed.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Algorithms and invariants
nodes.summary: An algorithm gives explicit steps; an invariant is a property maintained by those steps.
nodes.detail: Correctness needs a maintained invariant, a conclusion on termination, and a termination argument.
nodes.proof: Euclid’s algorithm preserves common divisors because a=qb+r implies d divides a and b exactly when d divides b and r. Nonnegative remainders strictly decrease until zero, so it terminates.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Convexity
nodes.summary: A convex set contains the segment joining any two of its points.
nodes.detail: For x,y in C and 0≤t≤1, require tx+(1−t)y to belong to C.
nodes.proof: The intersection of convex sets is convex: a segment between two points of the intersection lies in each set, hence in their intersection.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Differential equations
nodes.summary: A differential equation constrains an unknown function through its derivatives.
nodes.detail: Solving includes specifying a domain and checking any initial or boundary conditions.
nodes.proof: For y′=y and y(0)=1, y=eˣ is a solution because its derivative is itself and e⁰=1. This verifies the candidate; uniqueness needs a separate argument.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.

nodes.title: Iteration and dynamical systems
nodes.summary: Iterate a function repeatedly to study how states evolve.
nodes.detail: A fixed point satisfies f(x)=x. Other points may approach it, cycle, or behave differently.
nodes.proof: For xₙ₊₁=xₙ/2, induction gives xₙ=x₀/2ⁿ. Thus every real starting value tends to the fixed point zero.
nodes.extraction: Curated learning note and elementary example; not a formal verification or a claim about a manuscript’s dependencies.
